front_blocks.md: Define a **radian**.

back_blocks.md: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius of the circle.

cards.front_md: Define a **radian**.
cards.back_md: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius of the circle.

front_blocks.md: Define **angular displacement**.

back_blocks.md: The angle, in radians, swept out by an object as it moves around a circle, measured with respect to the centre of orbit.

cards.front_md: Define **angular displacement**.
cards.back_md: The angle, in radians, swept out by an object as it moves around a circle, measured with respect to the centre of orbit.

front_blocks.md: What is the equation linking angular displacement, arc length and radius?

back_blocks.md: $Δ θ = \frac{s}{r}$

cards.front_md: What is the equation linking angular displacement, arc length and radius?

front_blocks.md: How many radians are equivalent to 360°?

back_blocks.md: $2 π \text{rad} \approx 6 . 28 \text{rad}$

front_blocks.md: To convert an angle from degrees to radians, multiply the angle in degrees by **..........**.

back_blocks.md: To convert an angle from degrees to radians, multiply the angle in degrees by **π/180**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
An angle of one radian is the angle subtended when the arc length equals the **circumference** of the circle.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
An angle of one radian is subtended when the arc length equals the **radius** of the circle, not the circumference.

front_blocks.md: Define **angular velocity**.

back_blocks.md: The rate of change of angular displacement, given by $ω = \frac{Δθ}{Δt}$ It is a **vector** quantity, measured in rad s<sup>-1</sup>.

cards.front_md: Define **angular velocity**.
cards.back_md: The rate of change of angular displacement, given by $ω = \frac{Δθ}{Δt}$ It is a **vector** quantity, measured in rad s<sup>-1</sup>.

front_blocks.md: How is angular speed *ω* related to linear speed *v* and radius *r*?

back_blocks.md: $v = ω r$

cards.front_md: How is angular speed *ω* related to linear speed *v* and radius *r*?
cards.back_md: $v = ω r$

front_blocks.md: State two equations for angular speed *ω* in terms of the time period *T* and frequency *f*.

back_blocks.md: $ω = \frac{2π}{T} = 2 π f$

cards.front_md: State two equations for angular speed *ω* in terms of the time period *T* and frequency *f*.
cards.back_md: $ω = \frac{2π}{T} = 2 π f$

front_blocks.md: For two objects with the same linear speed, how does angular velocity change as the radius of orbit increases?

back_blocks.md: The object further from the centre of orbit (larger *r*) has a **smaller** angular velocity, since $ω = \frac{v}{r}$

cards.front_md: For two objects with the same linear speed, how does angular velocity change as the radius of orbit increases?

front_blocks.md: Angular velocity is a **..........** quantity, meaning it has both a magnitude and a direction.

back_blocks.md: Angular velocity is a **vector** quantity, meaning it has both a magnitude and a direction.

cards.front_md: Angular velocity is a **..........** quantity, meaning it has both a magnitude and a direction.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Angular frequency (*ω*) and frequency (*f*) have the same units.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Angular frequency *ω* is measured in **rad s**<sup>**-1**</sup>, while frequency *f* is measured in **Hz**, even though the two are related by $ω = 2 π f$

front_blocks.md: Define **centripetal acceleration**.

back_blocks.md: The acceleration of an object towards the centre of a circle, when the object moves around the circle at a constant speed.

cards.front_md: Define **centripetal acceleration**.
cards.back_md: The acceleration of an object towards the centre of a circle, when the object moves around the circle at a constant speed.

front_blocks.md: In deriving centripetal acceleration, what approximation is applied as the angular displacement θ tends to zero?

back_blocks.md: The **small angle approximation**: $\mathrm{sin} θ \approx θ$ (for very small angles, in radians).

cards.front_md: In deriving centripetal acceleration, what approximation is applied as the angular displacement θ tends to zero?

front_blocks.md: Centripetal acceleration is always directed **..........** the centre of the circle.

back_blocks.md: Centripetal acceleration is always directed **towards** the centre of the circle.

cards.front_md: Centripetal acceleration is always directed **..........** the centre of the circle.
cards.back_md: Centripetal acceleration is always directed **towards** the centre of the circle.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Because its speed is constant, an object in uniform circular motion has zero acceleration.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Speed being constant does not mean **velocity** is constant — the object's direction is continuously changing, so it has a centripetal acceleration directed towards the centre.

**False.**

front_blocks.md: Define **centripetal force**.

back_blocks.md: The resultant force towards the centre of the circle required to keep a body in uniform circular motion. It is always directed towards the centre of the body's rotation.

cards.front_md: Define **centripetal force**.
cards.back_md: The resultant force towards the centre of the circle required to keep a body in uniform circular motion. It is always directed towards the centre of the body's rotation.

front_blocks.md: Why does an object moving in a circle require a resultant force to act on it?

back_blocks.md: Because it is continuously changing **direction**, so it is not in equilibrium, even if its speed is constant.

cards.front_md: Why does an object moving in a circle require a resultant force to act on it?
cards.back_md: Because it is continuously changing **direction**, so it is not in equilibrium, even if its speed is constant.

front_blocks.md: In which direction do centripetal force and centripetal acceleration act, relative to each other?

back_blocks.md: In the **same direction**, towards the centre of the circle, following Newton's second law $F = m a$

cards.front_md: In which direction do centripetal force and centripetal acceleration act, relative to each other?
cards.back_md: In the **same direction**, towards the centre of the circle, following Newton's second law $F = m a$

front_blocks.md: Is centripetal force a distinct type of force?

back_blocks.md: No. Centripetal force is **not** a separate force in its own right — it is the name given to whichever resultant force (for example tension, gravity or magnetic force) keeps a body moving on a circular path.

front_blocks.md: The magnetic force on a charged particle can act as a **..........** force, since it always acts at 90° to the particle's velocity.

back_blocks.md: The magnetic force on a charged particle can act as a **centripetal** force, since it always acts at 90° to the particle's velocity.

cards.front_md: The magnetic force on a charged particle can act as a **..........** force, since it always acts at 90° to the particle's velocity.
cards.back_md: The magnetic force on a charged particle can act as a **centripetal** force, since it always acts at 90° to the particle's velocity.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Centripetal force is an additional force that acts alongside gravity, tension or other forces on an object moving in a circle.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Centripetal force is not an extra force added to the others — it is simply the name for the resultant of the existing forces (for example tension and gravity) that points towards the centre.

front_blocks.md: Define **centripetal force** in terms of its direction relative to motion.

back_blocks.md: A **centripetal force** is always directed perpendicular to an object's direction of travel, towards the centre of the circle.

front_blocks.md: State three equivalent equations for centripetal force *F*.

back_blocks.md: $F = \frac{mv^{2}}{r} = m r ω^{2} = m v ω$

front_blocks.md: In vertical circular motion, why does the tension in the string vary continuously as the object moves around the circle?

back_blocks.md: The **direction** of the tension changes as the object moves, while the direction of the **weight** stays constant, so the resultant (centripetal) force needed varies with position.

front_blocks.md: What speed condition, and tension value, define the minimum speed at the top of a vertical circle?

back_blocks.md: The minimum speed occurs when the string is taut but the tension is zero (*T* = 0), giving $v = \sqrt{gr}$

front_blocks.md: In vertical circular motion, the tension in the string is at its **..........** value at the bottom of the circle.

back_blocks.md: In vertical circular motion, the tension in the string is at its **maximum** value at the bottom of the circle.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In vertical circular motion, an object moves fastest at the top of the circle.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The object moves **slowest** at the top of the circle, where tension is at a minimum, and **fastest** at the bottom, where tension is at a maximum.
